title: Crack the Code
sub: Grades 3–4 · The Rosetta Stone Decoder · One message, three scripts

hero.credit: Hans Hillewaert, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

objective: Students will discover why the Rosetta Stone unlocked hieroglyphs: it carries one priestly decree three times, in hieroglyphic, demotic and Greek, and scholars could still read the Greek. Following the exhibition’s *Rosetta Stone Decoder*, they will use the Greek to read King Ptolemy’s name sign by sign, then test their code on Queen Cleopatra’s name, the way Jean-François Champollion did.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: For centuries nobody could read hieroglyphs. The Rosetta Stone let people do it again, because one thing on it could still be read. Cracking a name the way the code breakers did shows how a careful guess becomes proof.

materials: Page 3 of this plan, projected or printed: the stone, its three scripts and the two names
Differentiated handouts, one per student; optional devices for *The Rosetta Stone Decoder*
connection: **Virtual visit:** open *The Rosetta Stone Decoder* and follow its five steps: which writing can you read, find the king’s name, crack the code, check it with a queen, cracked!
**Poster 1** tells the stone’s story, and where it spent the First World War.

steps.title: Which writing can you read?
script: Show the whole stone without explanation. Ask: *“How many kinds of writing can you see? Could you read any of it?”* Pairs talk for a minute; someone may spot letters like ours at the bottom. Then read the room’s opening: *“In 1799, soldiers in Egypt found a broken stone. One message was carved on it three times, in three kinds of writing. By then, nobody could read hieroglyphs. But people could still read Greek.”*

screen.caption: The Rosetta Stone

steps.purpose: Look before anyone explains: three bands of writing, and one you might know.
students: How many kinds of writing can you see?
Is any of it writing you could read?

steps.title: One message, three scripts
script: Show the three bands on page 3. **Hieroglyphs** are the oldest Egyptian writing, used on temples, tombs and monuments. **Demotic**, a quicker handwritten script, was used for daily letters and literature. **Greek** became widespread after Alexander the Great conquered Egypt in 332 BC.

groups.label: Hieroglyphic
groups.text: The oldest. Used on temples, tombs and other monuments.

items.caption: Top
items.alt: The hieroglyphic band: rows of small pictures, with an oval around a few signs

groups.label: Demotic
groups.text: Handwritten, for daily letters and literature.

items.caption: Middle
items.alt: The demotic band: dense rows of flowing, joined-up marks

items.caption: Bottom
items.alt: The Greek band: rows of capital letters

steps.purpose: Meet the three scripts, and what each was used for.
students: Which script looks most like pictures?
Which one looks like joined-up handwriting?

steps.title: Found in 1799
script: In July 1799, French soldiers rebuilding an old fort at Rashid found the stone; Europeans called Rashid “Rosette”. It carries one priestly decree in each script, drawn up on 27 March 196 BC by a council of priests in Memphis, under Ptolemy V.

screen.alt: The Rosetta Stone Decoder room: the dark stone carved with its three scripts, beside the story of the one decree
screen.caption: The Rosetta Stone Decoder: one decree, three scripts

steps.purpose: Hear the stone’s story: where it was found, and what it says.
students: Why carve the same message three times?

steps.title: Find the king’s name
script: Scholars could still read Greek, and the Greek names the king: **Ptolemy**. Code breakers focused on the oval **cartouches** enclosing royal names: if the Greek says *Ptolemy*, the hieroglyphs should too.

screen.text:
Scholars could still read Greek.
The Greek text names the king: Ptolemy.

steps.purpose: See where the code breakers started: a name, in an oval.
students: In the hieroglyphs, find an oval with signs inside.

steps.title: Crack the code
script: Show the Greek name and the cartouche on page 3. Students count: ten Greek letters, seven signs. Work the first signs together: the stool is *p*, the loaf of bread *t*, the lasso *o*, the lion *l*. Let students finish: *m*, *i* (two reeds), *s* (a folded cloth). Ask: *“Which Greek letters have no sign?”* The vowels *E*, *A* and the second *O*.

examples.title: Ptolemy in Greek, and in hieroglyphs
steps: The Greek letters say P, T, O, L, E, M, A, I, O, S.
The cartouche has seven signs, in the same order.
Match them: P, T, O, L, M, I, S.
Three Greek letters have no sign: E, A and the second O.
examples.answer: Seven signs, seven sounds: P T O L M I S

steps.purpose: Crack the first name together: match sounds to signs, in order.
students: Count the Greek letters. Count the signs.
Which Greek letters have no sign?

steps.title: Your handout
script: Hieroglyphs were not an alphabet, though: one sign could stand for two or more sounds. Then students work on a handout.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Match the three scripts to their descriptions from a word bank, then crack Ptolemy’s name with the signs named and the Greek sounds given, and finish the stone’s story from a word bank.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Name the three scripts and what each was for, crack Ptolemy’s name and find the Greek letters with no sign, read three of Cleopatra’s signs with their new code, and explain why the Greek mattered.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Crack Ptolemy’s name, then test it on Cleopatra’s whole cartouche: fill in every sign they can, find the two different signs for *t*, explain the bread and egg that close her name, and say why a second name proves the code.

steps.purpose: Crack Ptolemy’s name on paper, then test the code, at the right level of challenge.
students: Everyone cracks Ptolemy. Then test your code on a queen.

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level student, who explains Cleopatra’s test.

steps.title: Look, I’ve got it!
script: Tell the ending. Thomas Young had read Ptolemy’s name, though not every sign correctly, and his work helped Champollion. On 14 September 1822, Champollion hurried to his brother, waving his notes: *“Look, I’ve got it!”* Close with poster 1’s question: *“If you wanted to leave a message that people could still understand thousands of years from now, how would you do it?”*
steps.purpose: End where the code breakers ended, and with a message for the future.
students: If you wanted to leave a message that people could still understand thousands of years from now, how would you do it?
